paras: The lynching of Green Harris, Giles Peck, John Woods and Burt Hoskins took place at about midnight in early March 1881 near New Haven Church, seven miles north of Jonesboro in Craighead County, Arkansas, when a band of masked men took the four Black prisoners from their guards and hanged them. The men had been accused of the murder of Mattie Ishmael, a planter's daughter, and committed to await the grand jury. Wire dispatches from Little Rock carried the story to papers across the country, most of which reported it as a just retribution.

On or about March 7, 1881, Benjamin Ishmael, described as a wealthy planter living a few miles from Jonesboro, returned from a mill to find his eighteen-year-old daughter dead on the floor of his house, beaten with an axe or club. The first dispatches said the motive was robbery, since Ishmael was supposed to keep a large sum hidden in the house, which had been searched without the money being found. "A number of negroes" were arrested, and the same dispatch predicted that "Judge Lynch will take a hand in the matter."

According to the Chicago Tribune's Little Rock dispatch, four of the arrested men were examined at New Haven Church before Justices of the Peace Akors and Jackson, who committed them to jail to await the grand jury at the coming circuit court. The hearing drew hundreds of people and lasted into the night, so the prisoners were kept in the church under guard, to be taken to the Jonesboro jail in the morning. Threats of lynching had been made, and although "many influential planters" urged that the law take its course, the guard was doubled.

At about midnight a body of masked men, estimated at 200 to 300, came out of the nearby woods and surrounded the building. They overpowered the guards, broke in the doors and windows, and dragged the four men to the nearest tree, which the Batesville Guard put about 200 yards away. The Tribune wrote that the prisoners begged for their lives and that all four were hanged on the same tree within fifteen minutes, after which the lynchers dispersed and left the bodies hanging. The wire added that "it is claimed" the men had made a full confession beforehand, saying the young woman was killed for refusing to reveal where her father's money was hidden.

No report of an inquest, of any arrest of the lynchers, or of grand jury action appears in the coverage. The Democrat's special said the lynching had intensified excitement in the neighborhood, while the Tribune reported that it had subsided and that "the better class of planters" deprecated the means used, though they held the murderers "deserved swift justice."

The news reached the national press through Little Rock specials to the St. Louis Republican and the New Orleans Democrat, which ran from Sacramento to Savannah between March 12 and 14. Southern headlines treated the hanging as deserved punishment, among them the Memphis Daily Appeal's "Swift Punishment Meted Out to the Negroes who Murdered Miss Ishmael" and the Savannah Morning News's "The Victim Avenged." The Chicago Tribune's headline, "Miss Ishmael Avenged," spoke of "her supposed murderers," and the Batesville Guard in Arkansas wrote that the murder had been "most terribly avenged."

Weekly papers condensed the story to a line, sometimes garbling it: one placed the lynching at Little Rock, another in Tennessee, and the St. Paul Daily Globe headlined the men as "Accused of Rape" although its text mentioned only murder. Several briefs repeated the confession as fact ("They confessed the crime"), and the Kenosha Telegraph wrote that the first day's testimony showed their guilt "very clearly" before "the citizens" hanged them.

Dissent came in commentary rather than news columns. The Indianapolis Leader reprinted the New York Herald's remark that "any white rascal" in the South could escape justice "by having a Negro lynched" and urged southern white men to put down the "hoodlum white element." In San Juan, the Boletín Mercantil described Jonesboro's residents as wanting their own sensational spectacle and closed with "¡Y viva la libertad!"

Accounts differ on where the prisoners were held: the Tribune named New Haven Church, the wire said a house or building, and the Spanish-language item said a jail. The night of the hanging is also uncertain, since the dispatches are dated March 11 and the weekly briefs said only "Friday." The reported confession rests on unnamed sources at the scene.

reader.title: Lynching of Green Harris, Giles Peck, John Woods and Burt Hoskins
bases: Four Black prisoners accused of murder were taken from guards by 200 to 300 masked men and hanged to a tree (A5, A18, A39).

All reports say the four men were hanged by a masked band of 200 to 300 that overpowered their guards (A5, A18), after a preliminary examination had committed them to await the grand jury (A18, A39), in punishment for the murder of which they were accused (A7, A19).

Separate Little Rock specials to the St. Louis Republican and the New Orleans Democrat (A5, A6, A19) and a fuller Chicago Tribune dispatch with details absent from both (A18) agree on the core event; no report denies it.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire (Republican and Democrat specials)
accounts.gist: Masked men, 200 to 300, came from the woods, surrounded the house or building where the prisoners were temporarily held, overpowered the guards and hanged them to a nearby tree; 'it is claimed' they confessed beforehand that the girl was killed for refusing to reveal where money was hidden.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune Little Rock dispatch
accounts.gist: After a crowded examination at New Haven Church before two justices, the men were committed for the grand jury and held overnight in the church under a doubled guard; at midnight the masked crowd smashed in, dragged them to the nearest tree and hanged all four on it within fifteen minutes, leaving the bodies hanging.

accounts.label: Kenosha Telegraph digest
accounts.gist: The 'first day's testimony' showed their guilt 'very clearly'; held in a church under strong guard, they were hanged to trees 'by the citizens' a few hours later.

accounts.label: Boletín Mercantil (quoting an unnamed paper)
accounts.gist: Jonesboro residents assaulted the jail, broke down doors, frightened the jailer and took the four to a tree.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Little Rock wire or a one-line digest of it, under headlines such as 'Four Negroes Lynched in Arkansas' and 'Lynch-Law in Arkansas'.

Southern and some northern headlines cast the hanging as retribution and called the accused the murderers: 'Swift Punishment Meted Out to the Negroes who Murdered Miss Ishmael', 'The Victim Avenged', 'Miss Ishmael Avenged'; the Batesville Guard said the murder 'has been most terribly avenged'.
The Chicago Tribune dramatized the scene and reported planters' disapproval of the means while they held the murderers deserved 'swift justice'.
The Indianapolis Leader reprinted the New York Herald's suggestion that lynching lets 'any white rascal' escape by having a Negro lynched, and called for putting down the 'hoodlum white element'.
The Boletín Mercantil of San Juan treated it with irony as Jonesboro's 'espectáculo de sensacion' and closed '¡Y viva la libertad!'.

info: At about midnight on a night shortly before the Little Rock dispatches of March 11, 1881; weekly briefs give 'Friday' (March 11), and the Herald quoted in A36 said 'yesterday'. The exact night is not stated.

A tree near New Haven Church, seven miles north of Jonesboro, where the prisoners were held after their examination (A18); 'a tree about 200 yards away' from the building (A39); wire: 'the house where the negroes were temporarily placed' (A5); a Spanish-language paper says a jail (A42).
Green Harris, Giles Peck, John Woods and Burt Hoskins, four Black men; spellings vary (Pecke, 'Olles Beck', Hawes, Jud Woods, Haskins, Harkins, Horkins).

Accused of murdering Miss Mattie (also 'Mollie', 'Hattie') Ishmael, 18, daughter of planter Benjamin Ishmael, beaten to death in her father's house during his absence at a mill, reportedly in an attempt to rob money hidden in the house. One headline called it rape; no text says so.
A band of masked men who came from the nearby woods and dispersed silently; unnamed. A32 says 'the citizens'.
